title: The body: the charnel ground
hook: a body one day dead, two days, three; this body too is of that nature (MN 10), offered gently

segments.voice: Yesterday: the body, as four elements: earth, water, fire, air. Did you feel all four in one drink? Day two hundred fifty-five, the last exercise on the body.

A quick word before today. The last body exercise in the sutta is about death, and it's direct. If you're grieving right now, or today just isn't the day, it's completely fine to listen lightly, or to spend the practice with your breath instead. Nothing is lost. For everyone else: most of us live as if our own body were the one exception. Other people get old. Other people die. Somehow, not quite me. The sutta asks us to look at that gently, and honestly. Today: the body, the charnel ground.
screen: `A GENTLE NOTE FIRST.` → `THE ONE EXCEPTION.` → `THE CHARNEL GROUND.`

segments.voice: In ancient India, a charnel ground was a place outside town where bodies were left, rather than buried or burned. Monks and nuns sometimes went there to practice. The sutta describes a practitioner who sees a body there: one day dead, two days, three. Then, over nine stages, it describes what happens next, until at last there are only scattered bones, bleached white, and finally bones crumbled to dust. At each stage the practitioner turns to their own body and reflects: this body too is of the same nature. It will become like that. It is not exempt. That's the line the whole exercise rests on: this body too. It sounds grim, but look at what it's for. It isn't meant to frighten, or to make life feel worthless. In Buddhist teaching, remembering death, maranasati, is meant to wake you up to what matters. The Buddha is remembered as saying that mindfulness of death, well practiced, is of great fruit. If this body won't last forever, then the call you keep postponing matters. The grudge you're carrying weighs more than it's worth. And the ordinary morning you're living right now is precious, exactly because it's passing. Many practitioners say this reflection, done gently, leaves them calmer, not sadder. The fear of death is often loudest when we refuse to look at it. And notice: the chorus comes back even here. Arising and passing away. The body is the clearest example there is.
screen: `A CHARNEL GROUND OUTSIDE TOWN.` · `NINE STAGES, DOWN TO DUST.` · `IT IS NOT EXEMPT.` · `REMEMBERING DEATH WAKES YOU UP.` · then, large: `THIS BODY TOO.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and feel your body breathing. It's alive, warm, working. Quietly, if it feels right, reflect: this body too will not last forever. Let the thought be soft, not frightening. Then ask one question: given that, what matters today? Let an answer come, or not. If this feels too heavy right now, just rest with the breath instead. The bell holds the time.
The body, the charnel ground. Seeing another body return to dust, the practitioner reflects: this body too is of that nature.
Your line: this body too. Today, do one thing you've been putting off because you assumed there'd always be time. Day two hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Reflection on death (maranasati) is practiced across Buddhist traditions; in Thailand and Sri Lanka some monastics still contemplate bodies or skeletons, while most lay practitioners reflect quietly that this body, too, will not last.

fork.setup: you're a monk at the charnel ground, looking at a body three days dead. what does the sutta ask you to do next?
options: look away and think of something pleasant.
turn to your own body: this too is of the same nature.
pray for the dead person's rebirth.
fork.reveal: at every stage the practitioner applies what they see to their own body: it will become like that; it is not exempt.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditating on corpses is morbid.
what it means: seeing gently that this body too will pass, so today matters.
what a scholar hears: MN 10 gives nine charnel-ground contemplations (sīvathikā); the Buddha's praise of maraṇasati as 'of great fruit' is in AN 6.19–20.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the nine charnel-ground contemplations
